importance_rationale: The candidate is the QCD critical point problem under its authoritative literature formulation: Nagata's 2022 review (Prog. Part. Nucl. Phys. 127, 103991, Sec. 1.1.1) states verbatim that even the existence of the critical point is not established and that a first-principles QCD study is needed to establish existence or non-existence and, if it exists, the critical temperature and density. The candidate title, statement, and scope reproduce that formulation exactly (formulation_alignment: exact), with no scoped variant substituted under the famous name, so the named-problem check raises no mismatch. This is one of the central open problems of strong-interaction physics: the source itself documents that the sign problem defeats importance sampling precisely in the relevant region, which is why the problem is open rather than routine. It clearly merits the expensive later-literature audit, both to confirm current-open status against post-2022 work (e.g., functional methods, thimble and complex Langevin progress, BES-II experimental constraints) and to test whether any narrower surviving core needs recording.
scientific_significance_rationale: Solving this problem would fix the qualitative structure of the QCD phase diagram at finite baryon density — whether a first-order transition line terminating in a critical endpoint exists at all — which is currently unknown from first principles. A positive answer with quantified critical temperature and density would (a) give heavy-ion collision programs (RHIC Beam Energy Scan, FAIR, NICA) a first-principles target to aim experimental searches at, replacing model-dependent extrapolations; (b) constrain the equation of state of dense baryonic matter relevant to neutron-star structure and mergers; and (c) require a demonstrably controlled method for the finite-density sign problem, a capability that would transfer to other sign-problem-afflicted theories (dense matter systems, real-time dynamics, some condensed-matter models). A rigorous exclusion or no-go result would be comparably consequential: it would redirect a major experimental search program and reshape the accepted phase diagram. The score is 9 rather than 10 because the deliverable is a specific structural feature of one theory's phase diagram rather than a bound or mechanism of universal scope, though the methodological spillover is substantial.
expected_result: A correct final submission is a first-principles determination, faithful to the source's conditional two-part question. Branch 1 (existence established): a controlled QCD-based calculation demonstrating a critical endpoint in the temperature–baryon-chemical-potential phase diagram, reporting its critical temperature and density with documented statistical and systematic uncertainties (including continuum and finite-volume control appropriate to the method used) and explicit evidence that the sign problem at nonzero chemical potential is controlled rather than assumed away. Branch 2 (existence excluded): a controlled first-principles calculation excluding a critical point in the relevant region of the phase diagram, with the region of exclusion and its uncertainties stated. Branch 3 (rigorous no-go): a proof-level result establishing non-existence (or constraining existence) from QCD itself. In all branches the submission answers the source question directly — existence or non-existence first, then location if existent — and phenomenological model estimates alone do not qualify, matching the source's demand for a first-principles study.
verification_standard: The submission is checked against the source-faithful question: does a QCD critical point exist, and if so at what critical temperature and density, from first principles. A submission passes if and only if it is one of the following, with each component reviewed as a separate checkable unit of the same problem: (1) Existence plus location — a first-principles QCD calculation that (a) establishes a critical endpoint with quantified critical temperature and density, (b) documents statistical and systematic uncertainties including continuum and volume control appropriate to the method, and (c) demonstrates that the sign problem at nonzero chemical potential is controlled within the claimed error budget; the existence conclusion and the (T, mu) values are checked as separate units. (2) Exclusion — a first-principles QCD calculation excluding a critical point over an explicitly stated region of the phase diagram, with the methodological control and uncertainties supporting that exclusion documented. (3) No-go — a rigorous proof establishing non-existence or an existence constraint from QCD. In every branch the reviewer verifies that the result is first-principles (phenomenological models alone fail), that no narrowing of the phase-diagram region or observable has been introduced to obtain a cheap check, and that the claimed conclusion follows under the stated control of errors. The standard does not prescribe which method may be used and does not redefine the question.
verification_difficulty_rationale: The result genuinely answers the source question only if the sign problem is demonstrably controlled, so the load-bearing derivations a Reviewer must inspect are the validity of the submitter's finite-density method (which by necessity departs from standard, sign-problem-defeated techniques), the error analysis supporting the claimed existence/location or exclusion, and the continuum and volume extrapolations. Cheapest branch first: a rigorous no-go proof would be a long, novel natural-language derivation chain (high D, near-holistic), so it is not the cheapest branch. A simulation-based establishment allows delegating reruns of submitted code under a pinned protocol (R) to reproduce quoted observables, but reproduction alone cannot settle the claim: the reviewer must still reconstruct why the method's treatment of the complex action is valid, check that uncertainty quantification covers the sign-problem-related systematics, and review substantial non-standard code for correctness rather than merely running it. That residual is a long, fragile, and novel connected chain, placing the score in the 7-9 band; 8 reflects that the method-validity and error-control arguments are mutually dependent and technique-novel, while bounded replay of the numerical pipeline removes part of the burden. Limits that remain after review: results hold within the documented region, precision, and systematic budget; no branch can certify more than that. The score is descriptive metadata only and does not gate this high-importance problem.
